title: C Programming
summary: Learn C from your very first printf to pointers, dynamic memory, structs, files and safe professional code. Understand how computers really work.

lessons.title: Your first C program
lessons.summary: Write, compile and run a program that prints text.

slides.title: Welcome to C
slides.text:
**C** is a small, fast language created in 1972.
- It powers operating systems, databases and tiny devices
- Many languages (C++, Java, Python) borrowed its ideas
- Learning C shows you how a computer really works
slides.narration: Welcome to C! C was created in the early nineteen seventies, and it still runs much of the world, from operating systems to microwaves. Learning it teaches you how memory and programs really work underneath.

slides.title: The smallest useful program
slides.text: Every C program starts running at **main**.
slides.narration: Here is a complete C program. It includes a library for input and output, defines a function called main, prints one line, and returns zero to say everything went fine.

slides.title: Line by line
slides.text:
- `#include <stdio.h>` loads the standard input/output library
- `int main(void)` is where the program begins
- `printf(...)` prints text
- `\n` means *new line*
- `return 0;` tells the system "success"
- Every statement ends with a **semicolon**
slides.narration: Let's read it line by line. The include line brings in printf. Main is the entry point. The backslash n inside the text starts a new line, and return zero reports success. Notice that each statement ends with a semicolon.

slides.title: Printing several lines
slides.text: You can call `printf` many times, or put several `\n` in one string.
slides.narration: You can call printf as many times as you like. Text only moves to a new line when you print a newline character, so remember to add it at the end.

slides.title: Run it
slides.text:
Press **Run**. The editor:
1. **Compiles** your code into a program
2. **Runs** it and shows the output
Typos are reported as *compile errors* with a line number.
slides.narration: When you press Run, the editor first compiles your source code into a real program, then runs it. If you made a typo, the compiler stops and tells you the line where it found the problem.

lessons.notes:
## Your first program

A C program is a text file (ending in `.c`) that a **compiler** turns into a runnable program.

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    printf("Hello, world!\n");
    return 0;
}
```

## The parts

- **`#include <stdio.h>`** adds the *standard input/output* library. Without it, the compiler does not know `printf`.
- **`int main(void)`** is the function where execution starts. `int` means it returns a whole number; `void` means it takes no inputs.
- **Curly braces `{ }`** group the statements that belong to `main`.
- **`printf("...")`** prints text. Text in double quotes is called a *string*.
- **`\n`** is an *escape sequence* meaning "new line". Others: `\t` (tab), `\\` (backslash), `\"` (quote).
- **`return 0;`** ends `main` and reports success to the operating system.

## Common beginner mistakes

- Forgetting the **semicolon** at the end of a statement.
- Forgetting `\n`, so the next output sticks to the same line.
- Writing `Printf` - C is **case sensitive**, so it must be `printf`.

## Reading input

Most exercises read input. `scanf("%99s", name)` reads one word into a text buffer:

```c
char name[100];
scanf("%99s", name);
printf("Hello, %s!\n", name);
```

You will learn exactly how this works in the next lessons. For now, copy the pattern.

quiz.q: Where does a C program start running?
options: At the first line of the file
quiz.explain: Execution always begins in the main function.

quiz.q: What does \n do inside a string?
quiz.explain: Backslash n is the newline escape sequence.

quiz.q: What does return 0; in main mean?
quiz.explain: By convention, returning 0 from main means success.

exercise.title: Say hello
exercise.prompt:
Read one word (a name) from standard input and print `Hello, NAME!` followed by a newline.

Example: input `Ana` -> output `Hello, Ana!`

lessons.title: How C programs are built
lessons.summary: Understand compiling, errors, warnings and comments.

slides.title: From text to program
slides.text:
1. You write **source code** (`main.c`)
2. The **compiler** (gcc, clang) checks and translates it
3. You get an **executable** the CPU can run
C is *compiled*, not interpreted.
slides.narration: C is a compiled language. A program called the compiler reads your whole source file, checks it, and translates it into machine code. The result is an executable file that runs directly on the processor.

slides.title: Compile errors
slides.text:
The compiler refuses code it cannot understand:
- missing `;` or `}`
- misspelled names
- wrong types
Read the **first** error first: later ones are often side effects.
slides.narration: If your code breaks the rules of the language, the compiler stops with an error and a line number. Always fix the first error first, because one mistake often causes several confusing messages after it.

slides.title: Warnings matter
slides.text:
Warnings mean "this compiles, but looks wrong".
Professionals compile with `-Wall -Wextra` and fix **every** warning.
slides.narration: Warnings are different. The program still builds, but the compiler thinks something looks suspicious, like an unused variable or a wrong format. Good programmers treat warnings as bugs waiting to happen.

slides.title: Comments
slides.text: Comments are ignored by the compiler and explain *why*.
slides.narration: Comments are notes for humans. A double slash comments to the end of the line, and slash star starts a block comment that ends with star slash.

slides.title: Runtime errors
slides.text:
Some bugs only appear when the program **runs**:
- dividing by zero
- reading memory you do not own
- wrong logic giving wrong output
Test with several inputs!
slides.narration: Not every bug is caught by the compiler. Runtime errors happen while the program runs, such as dividing by zero or wrong logic. That is why we test programs with several different inputs.

lessons.notes:
## The build pipeline

C source code goes through several steps before it runs:

1. **Preprocessor** - handles lines starting with `#`, like `#include`, by pasting in header files.
2. **Compiler** - translates C into machine instructions and checks types and syntax.
3. **Linker** - joins your code with library code (like `printf`) into one **executable**.

On the command line this is usually one command:

```
gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 main.c -o main
./main
```

Averroes Code does this for you when you press **Run**.

## Errors vs warnings

| Kind | When | Example |
|------|------|---------|
| Compile error | Build stops | missing `;` |
| Warning | Builds, but suspicious | `printf("%d", 3.5)` |
| Runtime error | While running | divide by zero |
| Logic error | Wrong answer | using `+` instead of `*` |

Read the **first** compiler message carefully. It names the file, the line and the column.

## Comments

```c
// single-line comment
/* multi-line
   comment */
```

Write comments that explain **why** you do something, not what each obvious line does.

## Good habits

- Compile often, after small changes.
- Turn on warnings and fix them all.
- Test with normal, small and edge-case inputs.

quiz.q: Which tool turns C source code into machine code?
quiz.explain: The compiler (with the linker) produces the executable.

quiz.q: What should you fix first when you see many compile errors?
quiz.explain: Later errors are often caused by the first one.

quiz.q: Which is a comment in C?
quiz.explain: Double slash starts a line comment in C.

exercise.title: Doubled
exercise.prompt:
Read one integer `n` from standard input and print `n doubled is X` where X is `2 * n`.

Example: input `21` -> output `21 doubled is 42`

lessons.title: Variables and types
lessons.summary: Store numbers and characters in typed variables.

slides.title: What is a variable?
slides.text:
A **variable** is a named box in memory.
In C every box has a **type** that says what it can hold.
slides.narration: A variable is a named place in memory where you keep a value. In C, you must say what type of value goes in the box before you use it.

slides.title: Common types
slides.text:
- `int` - whole numbers: `-3`, `42`
- `long long` - very big whole numbers
- `double` - decimals: `3.14`
- `char` - one character: `'x'`
- `bool` - `true`/`false` (with `<stdbool.h>`)
slides.narration: The most common types are int for whole numbers, double for numbers with decimals, and char for a single character. For really large whole numbers use long long.

slides.title: Declare, assign, change
slides.text: A variable can change; `const` makes it read-only.
slides.narration: You declare a variable once, then you can assign new values to it later. If a value should never change, mark it const, and the compiler will stop you from changing it by accident.

slides.title: Always initialize
slides.text:
An uninitialized local variable holds **garbage**.
`int x; printf("%d", x);` prints an unpredictable value.
Give every variable a starting value.
slides.narration: Here is an important C rule. A local variable that you do not initialize contains whatever bits were left in memory. So always give your variables a starting value.

slides.title: Names and sizes
slides.text:
- Names: letters, digits, `_`; cannot start with a digit
- Case matters: `total` and `Total` differ
- `sizeof(int)` is usually **4** bytes, `sizeof(double)` **8**
slides.narration: Variable names can use letters, digits and underscores, but they cannot start with a digit, and capital letters matter. The sizeof operator tells you how many bytes a type uses.

lessons.notes:
## Variables

A variable has a **type**, a **name** and a **value**:

```c
int count = 0;
double temperature = 21.5;
char letter = 'C';
```

## Main types

| Type | Holds | Typical size |
|------|-------|--------------|
| `char` | one character / small number | 1 byte |
| `int` | whole numbers (about +-2 billion) | 4 bytes |
| `long long` | huge whole numbers | 8 bytes |
| `double` | decimal numbers | 8 bytes |
| `bool` | `true` / `false` (`#include <stdbool.h>`) | 1 byte |

Characters use **single quotes** (`'A'`), strings use **double quotes** (`"Hi"`).

## Assignment

`=` means "store the value on the right into the box on the left":

```c
int x = 3;
x = x + 1;   // x is now 4
```

## Constants

```c
const int DAYS_IN_WEEK = 7;
```

The compiler rejects any attempt to change a `const`.

## Initialize everything

In C, a local variable without a starting value contains garbage. Reading it is a bug called *undefined behavior*. Always write `int total = 0;` instead of `int total;`.

## Naming tips

- Use clear names: `width`, `studentCount`, `max_speed`.
- Avoid single letters except for loop counters like `i`.
- Names are case sensitive.

quiz.q: Which type best stores 3.75?
quiz.explain: double stores numbers with a fractional part.

quiz.q: What does an uninitialized local int contain?
quiz.explain: Uninitialized locals hold leftover memory; reading them is undefined behavior.

quiz.q: Which is a valid variable name?
quiz.explain: Names use letters, digits and underscores, cannot start with a digit, and cannot be keywords.

lessons.title: Input and output with printf and scanf
lessons.summary: Format output and read typed input safely.

slides.title: printf placeholders
slides.text:
`printf` fills **format specifiers** with values:
- `%d` int, `%lld` long long
- `%f` double, `%.2f` two decimals
- `%c` char, `%s` string, `%%` a percent sign
slides.narration: Printf takes a format string with placeholders, then the values to put in them. Percent d is for integers, percent f for doubles, percent c for a character and percent s for a string.
slides.code:
int qty = 3; double price = 2.5;
printf("%d items cost %.2f\n", qty, qty * price);

slides.title: Width and alignment
slides.text: Numbers between `%` and the letter control layout.
slides.narration: You can control the width of each value. A number sets the minimum width, a minus sign aligns to the left, and a leading zero pads with zeros, which is great for times and tables.

slides.title: Reading with scanf
slides.text:
`scanf` reads typed values from input.
Give it the **address** of each variable with `&`.
slides.narration: Scanf is the opposite of printf: it reads values. Because it needs to store into your variables, you pass their addresses using the ampersand sign. For doubles, scanf uses percent l f.
slides.code:
int age; double height;
scanf("%d %lf", &age, &height);

slides.title: Check what scanf returns
slides.text:
`scanf` returns **how many** values it read.
- `== 2` everything OK
- `EOF` input ended
Always check it in real programs.
slides.narration: Scanf returns how many values it successfully read. If the user typed letters instead of a number, it returns less than you expected. Checking this value is how real programs avoid working with garbage.

slides.title: Strings need a limit
slides.text:
`char name[50]; scanf("%49s", name);`
- no `&` for arrays
- `%49s` stops after 49 chars, leaving room for the end marker
- `%s` reads **one word**
slides.narration: When you read a word into a character array, write a width limit like forty nine, one less than the array size. Without it, a long input can overflow memory. Note that percent s reads only one word.

lessons.notes:
## printf

```c
printf("format", value1, value2, ...);
```

| Specifier | Type |
|-----------|------|
| `%d` | `int` |
| `%lld` | `long long` |
| `%f`, `%.2f` | `double` (2 decimals) |
| `%c` | `char` |
| `%s` | string |
| `%zu` | `size_t` (from `sizeof`) |
| `%%` | a literal `%` |

Flags: `%5d` (width 5, right-aligned), `%-5d` (left-aligned), `%05d` (zero-padded).

## scanf

```c
int a, b;
if (scanf("%d %d", &a, &b) != 2) {
    printf("Bad input\n");
    return 1;
}
```

- Pass **addresses**: `&a`. Arrays (strings) are already addresses, so no `&`.
- For `double` use **`%lf`** in scanf (but `%f` in printf).
- Spaces and newlines between numbers are skipped automatically.
- The return value is the number of items read, or `EOF` at end of input.

## Reading words safely

```c
char word[32];
scanf("%31s", word);   // at most 31 chars + the '\0' end marker
```

To read a whole line with spaces, use `fgets` (covered in the strings lesson).

## Rounding

`printf("%.2f", 2.675)` prints a value rounded to 2 decimals. Floating-point numbers are approximations, so tiny differences are normal.

quiz.q: Which specifier reads a double with scanf?
quiz.explain: scanf needs %lf for double; printf accepts %f.

quiz.q: Why do we write &x in scanf("%d", &x)?
options: scanf needs the address to store the value
quiz.explain: scanf writes into memory, so it needs the variable's address.

quiz.q: What does printf("%05d", 42) print?
quiz.explain: Width 5 with a 0 flag pads with zeros.

exercise.title: Shopping total
exercise.prompt:
Read a **price** (decimal number) and a **quantity** (integer) separated by a space.
Print `Total: X` where X is `price * quantity` with exactly two decimals.

Example: input `2.50 4` -> output `Total: 10.00`

lessons.title: Operators and expressions
lessons.summary: Do arithmetic, understand integer division and the modulo operator.

slides.title: Arithmetic
slides.text:
`+` `-` `*` `/` `%`
Normal math precedence: `*` `/` `%` before `+` `-`.
Use parentheses to be clear.
slides.narration: C has the usual arithmetic operators. Multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction, just like in school math. When in doubt, add parentheses.

slides.title: Integer division
slides.text:
When **both** sides are ints, `/` throws away the fraction.
`7 / 2` is **3**, not 3.5.
Make one side a double to keep decimals.
slides.narration: This surprises everyone once. Dividing two integers gives an integer, and the fraction is simply cut off. Seven divided by two is three. To get three point five, make one of them a double, for example with a cast.
slides.code:
int q = 7 / 2;               // 3
double r = 7 / 2.0;          // 3.5
double s = (double)7 / 2;    // 3.5 (cast)

slides.title: The remainder operator %
slides.text:
`a % b` gives the **remainder** of `a / b`.
- `7 % 2` is 1 -> odd number
- `n % 10` is the last digit
- `seconds % 60` -> leftover seconds
slides.narration: The percent operator gives the remainder after integer division. It is incredibly useful: check if a number is even, get its last digit, or split seconds into minutes and seconds.

slides.title: Shortcuts
slides.text: Compound assignment and increment save typing.
slides.narration: C has short forms. Plus equals adds to a variable, and plus plus adds one. You will see these everywhere, especially in loops.

slides.title: Overflow
slides.text:
An `int` has a limit (about 2.1 billion).
Going past it is **undefined behavior** for signed ints.
Use `long long` for big results.
slides.narration: Every integer type has a maximum. If a calculation goes beyond it, the result is wrong or undefined. When numbers can get large, like multiplying big values, use long long.

lessons.notes:
## Arithmetic operators

| Operator | Meaning | Example | Result |
|----------|---------|---------|--------|
| `+` | add | `5 + 2` | 7 |
| `-` | subtract | `5 - 2` | 3 |
| `*` | multiply | `5 * 2` | 10 |
| `/` | divide | `5 / 2` | **2** (ints) |
| `%` | remainder | `5 % 2` | 1 |

## Integer division

If both operands are integers, the result is an integer and the fraction is discarded (truncated toward zero). To get a decimal result, make one operand a `double`:

```c
double avg = (double)sum / count;
```

The `(double)` is a **cast**: it converts a value to another type.

## Using % (modulo)

```c
int total = 3725;            // seconds
int hours = total / 3600;    // 1
int minutes = total % 3600 / 60; // 2
int seconds = total % 60;    // 5
```

Other uses: `n % 2 == 0` checks for even numbers; `n % 10` gets the last digit.

## Compound assignment

`+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=` and `++`, `--`.

## Precedence

`*`, `/`, `%` bind tighter than `+`, `-`. Assignment `=` happens last. Use parentheses whenever an expression is not obvious.

## Overflow

`int` usually holds values from about -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647. Signed overflow is undefined behavior, so use `long long` (and `%lld`) for large values.

quiz.q: What is 17 / 5 in C when both are int?
quiz.explain: Integer division drops the fraction: 3.

quiz.q: What is 17 % 5?
quiz.explain: 17 = 3*5 + 2, so the remainder is 2.

quiz.q: After int x = 4; x *= 3; what is x?
quiz.explain: x *= 3 means x = x * 3.

exercise.title: Clock time
exercise.prompt:
Read a number of seconds `t` (0 <= t < 86400) and print it as `H:MM:SS`.
Hours are not padded; minutes and seconds always use two digits.

Example: input `3661` -> output `1:01:01`

lessons.title: Making decisions with if and switch
lessons.summary: Choose what the program does with if, else and switch.

slides.title: if and else
slides.text: Run code only when a condition is **true**.
slides.narration: An if statement checks a condition. If it is true, the first block runs. Otherwise the else block runs. In C, any non-zero value counts as true and zero is false.

slides.title: Comparison operators
slides.text:
`==` equal, `!=` not equal
`<` `<=` `>` `>=`
Careful: `=` **assigns**, `==` **compares**!
slides.narration: To compare values use double equals, not a single one. A single equals sign assigns a value, and writing it inside an if is a classic bug that compilers warn about.

slides.title: else if chains
slides.text: Test several cases in order; the first true one wins.
slides.narration: When there are several possibilities, chain else if blocks. C checks them from top to bottom and runs only the first one that is true.

slides.title: Combining conditions
slides.text:
- `&&` AND: both must be true
- `||` OR: at least one true
- `!` NOT: flips true/false
`if (age >= 13 && age <= 19)` -> teenager
slides.narration: You can combine conditions. Double ampersand means and, two vertical bars mean or, and the exclamation mark means not. C stops evaluating as soon as it knows the answer, which is called short circuiting.

slides.title: switch
slides.text: `switch` picks a case by an integer or char value.
slides.narration: A switch statement compares one value against several constants. Each case usually ends with break. Without break, execution falls through into the next case, which is rarely what you want.

quiz.q: Which operator compares two values for equality?
quiz.explain: == compares; = assigns.

quiz.q: What happens if you forget break in a switch case?
options: Execution falls through to the next case
quiz.explain: Without break, control continues into the following case.

quiz.q: When is (a > 0 || b > 0) true?
options: If at least one is positive
quiz.explain: || needs at least one true operand.

exercise.title: Letter grade
exercise.prompt:
Read an integer score from 0 to 100 and print its grade:

- 90 or more: `A`
- 80-89: `B`
- 70-79: `C`
- 60-69: `D`
- below 60: `F`

lessons.title: Repeating with while and for
lessons.summary: Repeat work with while, do-while and for loops.

slides.title: Why loops?
slides.text:
Loops repeat code **without copying it**.
- print 1 to 100
- add up many numbers
- keep asking until input is valid
slides.narration: Programs often need to do the same thing many times. Instead of copying code, we write a loop that repeats a block while a condition stays true.

slides.title: while
slides.text: Repeats **while** the condition is true.
slides.narration: A while loop checks its condition first. If it is true, the body runs, and then it checks again. Make sure something in the body changes, or the loop will never end.

slides.title: for
slides.text: The counting loop: start; condition; step.
slides.narration: The for loop puts the three parts of counting on one line: where to start, when to keep going, and how to step. It is the most common loop in C.

slides.title: Accumulating
slides.text: A classic pattern: start a total at 0 and add inside the loop.
slides.narration: A very common pattern is the accumulator. Start a total at zero, then add to it on every turn of the loop. Use long long if the total might get large.

slides.title: do-while
slides.text:
`do { ... } while (cond);`
The body runs **at least once**, then the condition is checked.
Great for menus and "ask again" input.
slides.narration: The do while loop checks its condition at the end, so the body always runs at least once. It is handy for menus, where you always show the menu before asking whether to continue.

slides.title: Infinite loops
slides.text:
If the condition never becomes false, the loop runs forever.
- forgot `i++`
- wrong direction: `i--` instead of `i++`
Press **Stop** if your program hangs.
slides.narration: If you forget to update the counter, the condition never changes and the loop runs forever. If your program seems frozen, that is usually why. Stop it and check how the loop variable changes.

quiz.q: How many times does for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) run?
quiz.explain: i takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3: four times.

quiz.q: Which loop always runs its body at least once?
quiz.explain: do-while checks the condition after the body.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of an infinite loop?
options: Forgetting to update the loop variable
quiz.explain: If the variable never changes, the condition never becomes false.

exercise.title: Sum to n
exercise.prompt:
Read an integer `n` (0 <= n <= 1000000) and print the sum `1 + 2 + ... + n`.
For `n = 0` print `0`. Use a loop and `long long`.

lessons.title: Loop control and reading until the end
lessons.summary: Use break, continue, nested loops and read input until it runs out.

slides.title: break
slides.text: `break` leaves the loop **immediately**.
slides.narration: Break jumps out of the nearest loop right away. Use it when you have found what you were searching for and there is no need to keep going.

slides.title: continue
slides.text: `continue` skips to the **next** iteration.
slides.narration: Continue skips the rest of the current turn and goes straight to the next one. Here we skip every number that is a multiple of three.

slides.title: Nested loops
slides.text: A loop inside a loop: rows and columns.
slides.narration: You can put one loop inside another. The inner loop runs completely for every single turn of the outer loop. This is how you print grids, tables and patterns.

slides.title: Reading until input ends
slides.text:
`scanf` returns **1** when it read a number.
At the end of input it returns `EOF`.
So `while (scanf("%d", &x) == 1)` processes every number.
slides.narration: Often you do not know how many numbers will come. The trick is to loop while scanf successfully reads one value. When the input runs out, scanf returns end of file and the loop stops.

slides.title: Tracking a maximum
slides.text:
Start `max` with the **first** value, not 0.
Otherwise all-negative inputs give a wrong answer.
slides.narration: To find the largest value, remember the best so far and update it whenever you see something bigger. Start with the first value you read, not with zero, or negative inputs will fool you.

quiz.q: What does continue do?
quiz.explain: continue skips the remaining body for this iteration.

quiz.q: What does scanf return at the end of input?
quiz.explain: scanf returns EOF when no more input is available.

quiz.q: Nested loops with 4 outer and 5 inner iterations run the inner body how many times?

exercise.title: Number statistics
exercise.prompt:
Read integers until the end of input (there is at least one).
Print one line: `count=C sum=S max=M`.

Example: input `3 -2 10` -> output `count=3 sum=11 max=10`

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.summary: Split programs into reusable named pieces with parameters and return values.

slides.title: Why functions?
slides.text:
A **function** is a named block of code you can call again and again.
- avoid repeating yourself
- give a name to an idea
- test small pieces separately
slides.narration: As programs grow, main gets long and messy. Functions let you package a piece of work under a name, and then call it whenever you need it. You have already used one: printf.

slides.title: Defining a function
slides.text: Return type, name, parameters, body.
slides.narration: A function definition starts with the type of value it returns, then its name, then its parameters in parentheses. The return statement sends a value back to the caller.

slides.title: void and multiple parameters
slides.text:
- `void` return type: the function returns nothing
- Parameters are separated by commas
- Each parameter has its own type
slides.narration: A function that only does something, like printing, has the return type void. A function can take several parameters, each with its own type, separated by commas.

slides.title: Pass by value
slides.text:
C copies each argument into the parameter.
Changing the parameter does **not** change the caller's variable.
(Pointers, later, let you change it.)
slides.narration: In C, arguments are passed by value. The function receives a copy, so if it changes its parameter, the original variable in the caller stays the same. Later, pointers will let us change the original.

slides.title: Prototypes
slides.text: Declare a function before `main`, define it later.
slides.narration: The compiler reads from top to bottom, so it must know about a function before it is called. You can either define it above main, or write a short prototype at the top and the full body later.

slides.title: Scope
slides.text:
Variables declared inside a function are **local**.
They exist only while the function runs and are invisible elsewhere.
Prefer parameters over global variables.
slides.narration: Variables created inside a function are local. They are born when the function starts and disappear when it returns. Other functions cannot see them, which keeps your program safe and easy to reason about.

quiz.q: What does a void function return?
quiz.explain: void means no return value.

quiz.q: If a function changes its int parameter, what happens to the caller's variable?
quiz.explain: C passes arguments by value, so only the copy changes.

quiz.q: What is a function prototype?
options: A declaration of the function's signature before its body
quiz.explain: A prototype declares the name, return type and parameters.

lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.summary: Store many values of the same type in one indexed collection.

slides.title: Many values, one name
slides.text:
An **array** holds a fixed number of values of one type, side by side in memory.
`int scores[5];` -> 5 ints
slides.narration: An array stores many values of the same type under one name. They sit next to each other in memory, and you choose how many when you declare it.

slides.title: Indexing from zero
slides.text: The first element is `[0]`, the last is `[n-1]`.
slides.narration: Elements are numbered from zero. So an array of five elements has indexes zero to four. Using index five is outside the array, and C will not stop you, which is why you must be careful.

slides.title: Loop over an array
slides.text: A `for` loop from 0 to n-1 visits every element.
slides.narration: Arrays and for loops go together. Loop the index from zero while it is less than the length, and you visit every element exactly once.

slides.title: No bounds checking
slides.text:
C does **not** check indexes.
`a[10]` on a 5-element array reads or writes random memory.
This is a top source of crashes and security bugs.
slides.narration: Here is a critical difference from many languages. C never checks that your index is valid. Writing past the end silently damages other memory. Always keep your index inside the array.

slides.title: Passing arrays to functions
slides.text: Pass the array **and** its length.
slides.narration: When you pass an array to a function, the function receives the address of its first element and does not know the length. So always pass the length as a separate parameter.

lessons.notes:
## Declaring arrays

```c
int nums[5];                    // 5 ints, uninitialized
int primes[4] = {2, 3, 5, 7};   // initialized
int zeros[100] = {0};           // all zeros
double temps[] = {1.5, 2.5};    // size inferred: 2
```

## Indexes

Valid indexes are `0` to `n - 1`. The size is fixed when the array is created.

```c
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    printf("%d\n", nums[i]);
}
```

## Reading into an array

```c
int n;
scanf("%d", &n);
int a[1000];
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) scanf("%d", &a[i]);
```

Make sure `n` never exceeds the array size. (Dynamic memory, later, removes this limit.)

## Number of elements

For a real array in the same scope:
```c
size_t len = sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]);
```
This does **not** work inside a function that received the array as a parameter, because there it is only a pointer.

## Arrays and functions

```c
void print_all(const int a[], int n);
```
`const` promises not to modify the elements. Without `const`, the function **can** modify the caller's array, because arrays are not copied.

## 2D arrays

```c
int grid[3][4];      // 3 rows, 4 columns
grid[1][2] = 7;
```

## Danger: out of bounds

Accessing `a[n]` or `a[-1]` is undefined behavior: it may crash, or silently corrupt data.

quiz.q: What is the index of the last element in int a[8]?
quiz.explain: Indexes run from 0 to n-1.

quiz.q: What happens if you write to a[10] when a has 5 elements?
options: Undefined behavior: memory may be corrupted
quiz.explain: C does not check bounds.

quiz.q: Why pass the length to a function along with an array?
options: The function cannot know the array's length otherwise
quiz.explain: An array parameter is just a pointer; the size is lost.

lessons.title: Strings and characters
lessons.summary: Work with text stored as character arrays ending in a null byte.

slides.title: A string is a char array
slides.text:
C has no built-in string type.
A string is an array of `char` ending with `'\0'` (the **null terminator**).
`"Hi"` uses **3** bytes: `'H' 'i' '\0'`
slides.narration: C does not have a special string type. A string is just an array of characters, followed by a special zero character that marks the end. So the word Hi needs three bytes, not two.

slides.title: string.h helpers
slides.text: The `<string.h>` library does common jobs.
slides.narration: The string library gives you helpers. Strlen counts characters up to the terminator. Strcmp compares two strings and returns zero when they are equal. Never compare strings with double equals, because that compares addresses.

slides.title: Reading a whole line
slides.text: `fgets` reads a line, spaces included, and never overflows.
slides.narration: Scanf with percent s stops at a space. To read a whole line, use fgets with the buffer size. It keeps the newline at the end, so we remove it with strcspn.

slides.title: Characters are numbers
slides.text:
A `char` stores a small number (its ASCII code).
`'A'` is 65, `'a'` is 97, `'0'` is 48.
`<ctype.h>`: `isdigit`, `isalpha`, `toupper`, `tolower`
slides.narration: Each character is really a small number. Capital A is sixty five. That means you can loop over a string and test or change characters, using helpers like isdigit and toupper from the c type library.

slides.title: Looping over a string
slides.text: Stop at the null terminator.
slides.narration: To process a string, loop until you reach the terminator character. Here we turn every letter into a capital letter.

lessons.notes:
## Strings in C

```c
char name[10] = "Ada";   // 'A' 'd' 'a' '\0' + 6 unused bytes
```
The `'\0'` byte marks the end. Every string function relies on it.

## Useful functions (`#include <string.h>`)

| Function | Does |
|----------|------|
| `strlen(s)` | length without `'\0'` |
| `strcmp(a, b)` | 0 if equal, <0 or >0 for order |
| `strcpy(dst, src)` | copy (dst must be big enough) |
| `strcat(dst, src)` | append |
| `strchr(s, c)` | find a character |
| `strcspn(s, set)` | index of first char from set |

Safer alternatives: `snprintf(dst, size, "%s", src)` always respects the buffer size.

## Comparing

```c
if (a == b)            // WRONG: compares addresses
if (strcmp(a, b) == 0) // RIGHT: compares contents
```

## Reading text

- `scanf("%49s", word)` - one word, max 49 characters.
- `fgets(line, sizeof line, stdin)` - a whole line including spaces and the trailing `\n`. Returns `NULL` at end of input.

```c
line[strcspn(line, "\n")] = '\0';  // strip the newline
```

## Characters (`#include <ctype.h>`)

`isalpha`, `isdigit`, `isspace`, `isupper`, `islower`, `toupper`, `tolower`.
Cast to `unsigned char` when passing a `char`: `isdigit((unsigned char)c)`.

Digits to numbers: `'7' - '0'` equals `7`.

quiz.q: How many bytes does the string literal "cat" occupy?
quiz.explain: Three letters plus the '\0' terminator.

quiz.q: How do you correctly check if two C strings are equal?
quiz.explain: strcmp compares contents; == compares addresses.

quiz.q: Which function reads a whole line including spaces safely?
quiz.explain: fgets reads a line and respects the buffer size. gets was removed from C because it is unsafe.

lessons.title: Pointers
lessons.summary: Understand addresses, the * and & operators, and why pointers matter.

slides.title: Memory has addresses
slides.text:
Every variable lives at an **address** in memory.
`&x` gives the address of `x`.
A **pointer** is a variable that stores an address.
slides.narration: Memory is like a long street of numbered houses. Each variable lives at an address. The ampersand operator gives you that address, and a pointer is simply a variable that stores an address.

slides.title: Declaring and using a pointer
slides.text: `*` declares a pointer and also **follows** it.
slides.narration: We declare p as a pointer to int and store the address of x in it. Writing star p follows the pointer to the value it points to. Changing star p changes x itself.
slides.code:
int x = 10;
int *p = &x;     // p holds x's address
printf("%d\n", *p);  // 10 (dereference)
*p = 25;         // changes x
printf("%d\n", x);   // 25

slides.title: Changing the caller's variables
slides.text: Pass addresses to let a function modify variables.
slides.narration: Remember that functions get copies. If we pass addresses instead, the function can follow them and change the original variables. This is exactly why scanf needs ampersands.

slides.title: Pointers and arrays
slides.text:
An array name turns into a pointer to its first element.
`a[i]` is the same as `*(a + i)`.
Adding 1 to an `int *` moves to the **next int**.
slides.narration: Arrays and pointers are closely connected. An array's name acts as a pointer to its first element, and indexing is really pointer arithmetic. Adding one to a pointer moves it to the next element, not the next byte.

slides.title: NULL and dangers
slides.text:
`NULL` means "points to nothing".
- Never dereference `NULL` or an uninitialized pointer
- Initialize pointers: `int *p = NULL;`
- Check before use: `if (p != NULL)`
slides.narration: A pointer set to NULL points to nothing. Following a NULL pointer, or a pointer that was never set, crashes the program or worse. Always initialize your pointers and check them before use.

quiz.q: If int *p = &x;, what is *p?
quiz.explain: *p dereferences the pointer, giving x's value.

quiz.q: Why does swap need pointer parameters?
quiz.explain: With pointers, the function can change the originals.

quiz.q: a[i] is equivalent to:
quiz.explain: Indexing is pointer arithmetic followed by a dereference.

exercise.title: Min and max with pointers

Read `n` (1 <= n <= 1000) and then `n` integers. Print `min max` on one line.

lessons.title: Dynamic memory with malloc and free
lessons.summary: Allocate memory at runtime on the heap and release it correctly.

slides.title: Stack vs heap
slides.text:
- **Stack**: local variables, automatic, small, freed when the function ends
- **Heap**: you ask for memory with `malloc`, it lives until you `free` it
Use the heap when the size is known only at runtime.
slides.narration: Local variables live on the stack and disappear automatically. Sometimes you only know at runtime how much memory you need, or you need it to outlive a function. Then you ask for heap memory.

slides.title: malloc
slides.text: Ask for `n` elements, check for `NULL`.
slides.narration: Malloc takes a number of bytes and returns a pointer to fresh memory. Multiply the count by sizeof the element type. If memory runs out, malloc returns NULL, so always check.

slides.title: Use it like an array
slides.text: Heap memory works with normal indexing.
slides.narration: Once you have the pointer, you use it exactly like an array. Remember that malloc does not clear the memory, so set every element before reading it, or use calloc, which fills it with zeros.

slides.title: free
slides.text:
Every `malloc` needs exactly **one** `free`.
- Forgetting -> **memory leak**
- Freeing twice -> crash
- Using after free -> undefined behavior
Tip: set the pointer to `NULL` after freeing.
slides.narration: When you are done, give the memory back with free. Every allocation needs exactly one free. Forgetting it leaks memory. Freeing twice, or using memory after freeing it, are serious bugs.

slides.title: Growing with realloc
slides.text: `realloc` resizes a block, possibly moving it.
slides.narration: To grow an array, use realloc. It may move the data to a new place, so store the result in a temporary pointer first. If it fails, your old memory is still valid.

quiz.q: What must you do with memory from malloc when finished?
quiz.explain: Every malloc must be matched with a free.

quiz.q: What does malloc return when it fails?
quiz.explain: malloc returns NULL on failure.

quiz.q: What is a memory leak?
options: Allocated memory that is never freed
quiz.explain: Leaked memory stays reserved until the program exits.

lessons.title: Structs: grouping data
lessons.summary: Bundle related values into your own types with struct and typedef.

slides.title: Why structs?
slides.text:
A student has a name, an age and a score.
Keeping three separate arrays is messy.
A **struct** groups them into one new type.
slides.narration: Real things have several properties. A student has a name, an age and a score. Instead of juggling separate variables, a struct lets you group them into one new type.

slides.title: Defining a struct
slides.text: `typedef` gives the type a short name.
slides.narration: Here we define a struct with three members and use typedef to name it Student. Then we can create Student variables and reach each member with a dot.

slides.title: Arrays of structs
slides.text: A list of records, like rows in a table.
slides.narration: You can make arrays of structs, which works like a table where each element is a row. Loop over it just like any other array.

slides.title: Pointers to structs: ->
slides.text: `p->age` is short for `(*p).age`.
slides.narration: When you have a pointer to a struct, use the arrow operator to reach a member. Passing a pointer avoids copying the whole struct and lets the function change it.

slides.title: Structs are copied
slides.text:
Assigning or passing a struct **copies** all members.
- Pass `const Student *` for read-only access to big structs
- Pass `Student *` to modify
slides.narration: Unlike arrays, structs are copied when you assign them or pass them by value. For large structs, pass a const pointer to read, or a normal pointer when you want to modify it.

quiz.q: How do you access member age through a pointer p to a struct?
quiz.explain: The arrow operator dereferences and accesses a member.

quiz.q: What does typedef do in typedef struct {...} Student;?
options: Gives the struct type the name Student
quiz.explain: typedef creates an alias for a type.

quiz.q: What happens when you pass a struct by value?
quiz.explain: Structs are copied member by member.

lessons.title: Files and streams
lessons.summary: Read and write files with FILE pointers, and see that stdin and stdout are streams too.

slides.title: Streams
slides.text:
C talks to files through **streams** of type `FILE *`.
Three are always open:
- `stdin` keyboard / input
- `stdout` screen / output
- `stderr` error messages
slides.narration: In C, all input and output goes through streams. A stream is a FILE pointer. Three streams are always ready: standard input, standard output, and standard error for error messages.

slides.title: Opening a file
slides.text: `fopen(path, mode)` returns a `FILE *` or `NULL`.
slides.narration: To use a file, open it with fopen, giving the path and a mode. The mode r reads, w writes and erases old content, and a appends. If the file cannot be opened, fopen returns NULL, so always check.

slides.title: Reading lines
slides.text: `fgets` works on any stream.
slides.narration: Reading a file line by line uses fgets, the same function you used for keyboard input. It returns NULL at the end of the file, which makes a clean loop.

slides.title: Same code, any stream
slides.text:
`printf(...)` is `fprintf(stdout, ...)`
`scanf(...)` is `fscanf(stdin, ...)`
Write functions that take a `FILE *` and they work with files **and** the keyboard.
slides.narration: Here is a neat idea. Printf is just fprintf to standard output. If your function takes a FILE pointer, you can pass a real file or standard input, and the same code works for both. Our exercises use standard input this way.

slides.title: Always close
slides.text:
- `fclose(f)` flushes and releases the file
- Too many open files -> failure
- Unflushed data may be **lost** on a crash
slides.narration: When you are done, always close the file. Closing writes out any buffered data and frees system resources. Forgetting it can lose data or run out of file handles.

quiz.q: What does fopen return if the file cannot be opened?
quiz.explain: fopen returns NULL on failure.

quiz.q: Which mode erases an existing file before writing?
quiz.explain: "w" truncates the file.

quiz.q: Which stream should error messages go to?
quiz.explain: stderr is meant for diagnostics.

lessons.title: Memory safety and robust input
lessons.summary: Avoid the classic C bugs and validate input like a professional.

slides.title: Why C needs care
slides.text:
C trusts you completely. No bounds checks, no garbage collector.
Most serious security bugs in C come from:
- buffer overflows
- use after free
- uninitialized values
- integer overflow
slides.narration: C gives you full control and trusts you completely. That makes it fast, but it also means mistakes with memory can become crashes or security holes. Professionals use habits and tools to prevent them.

slides.title: Buffer overflows
slides.text: Always limit how much you write into a buffer.
slides.narration: A buffer overflow happens when you write more data than a buffer can hold. Use functions that take a size, like fgets and snprintf, and give scanf a width limit.
slides.code:
char name[16];
scanf("%s", name);           // UNSAFE: no limit
scanf("%15s", name);         // safe
snprintf(name, sizeof name, "%s", input);  // safe copy

slides.title: Validate numbers with strtol
slides.text: `strtol` tells you **where** parsing stopped.
slides.narration: Scanf happily reads twelve from twelve x and ignores the rest. Strtol gives you a pointer to where it stopped, so you can reject input that contains extra characters, and it reports values that are out of range.

slides.title: Let tools find bugs
slides.text:
- `-Wall -Wextra -Werror` : treat warnings as errors
- `-fsanitize=address,undefined` : catch overflows at runtime
- **Valgrind** : find leaks
- static analyzers : `clang-tidy`, `cppcheck`
slides.narration: You do not have to find every bug by hand. Compiler warnings, address sanitizer, Valgrind and static analyzers catch many memory errors automatically. Use them on every project.

slides.title: Defensive habits
slides.text:
1. Initialize every variable
2. Check every return value
3. Pass sizes with buffers
4. Free once, then set to `NULL`
5. Keep functions small and test edge cases
slides.narration: Here is a checklist of habits. Initialize everything, check every return value, always pass buffer sizes, free memory exactly once, and test edge cases like empty input and huge numbers.

quiz.q: Which call is safe for reading a word into char name[16]?
quiz.explain: %15s leaves room for the '\0' terminator.

quiz.q: Why is strtol better than atoi for validation?
options: It reports where parsing stopped and range errors
quiz.explain: strtol's end pointer and errno let you detect bad input.

quiz.q: Which tool detects buffer overflows at runtime?
quiz.explain: -fsanitize=address instruments memory accesses.

lessons.title: Problem solving: sorting and searching
lessons.summary: Plan algorithms, use qsort and binary search, and think about speed.

slides.title: Think before typing
slides.text:
1. Understand the input and output exactly
2. Solve a tiny example **by hand**
3. Write the steps in plain words
4. Translate to C
5. Test edge cases: empty, one item, duplicates, negatives
slides.narration: Good programmers do not start by typing. They first understand the input and output, solve a small example by hand, and write the steps in plain words. Then the code almost writes itself.

slides.title: Big-O in one minute
slides.text:
How does work grow with input size **n**?
- `O(1)` constant: array index
- `O(log n)` binary search
- `O(n)` one loop
- `O(n log n)` good sorting
- `O(n^2)` nested loops
slides.narration: Big O notation describes how running time grows as the input grows. One loop over n items is order n. Two nested loops are order n squared, which gets slow quickly. Good sorting is order n log n.

slides.title: Sorting with qsort
slides.text: The standard library sorts any array; you supply a compare function.
slides.narration: C's standard library includes qsort. You give it the array, the count, the element size and a compare function. The compare function returns a negative, zero or positive number to describe the order.

slides.title: Binary search
slides.text: On **sorted** data, halve the search range each step.
slides.narration: Once data is sorted, binary search finds a value very fast. Look at the middle, then throw away the half that cannot contain the target. A million items need only about twenty steps.

slides.title: Where to go next
slides.text:
- Data structures: linked lists, stacks, hash tables, trees
- Multi-file projects with headers and **CMake**
- Systems programming: processes, sockets
- Embedded C on microcontrollers
slides.narration: Congratulations, you now know the core of C. Next you can build data structures like linked lists and hash tables, organize projects across many files, and explore systems or embedded programming.

lessons.notes:
## A problem-solving routine

1. **Read the task twice.** Write down the exact input and output format.
2. **Work an example by hand.**
3. **Choose data structures** (array? struct? sorted?).
4. **Write pseudocode**, then C.
5. **Test** normal cases and edge cases.

## Complexity

| Pattern | Cost | 1,000,000 items |
|---------|------|-----------------|
| index lookup | O(1) | 1 step |
| binary search | O(log n) | ~20 steps |
| single loop | O(n) | 1e6 steps |
| qsort | O(n log n) | ~2e7 steps |
| nested loops | O(n^2) | 1e12 steps - too slow |

## qsort

```c
#include <stdlib.h>

int cmp_int(const void *a, const void *b) {
    int x = *(const int *)a;
    int y = *(const int *)b;
    return (x > y) - (x < y);   // avoids overflow of x - y
}

qsort(arr, n, sizeof arr[0], cmp_int);
```

The compare function receives `const void *` pointers (generic pointers) that you cast to the real type. Sorting descending? Swap `x` and `y`.

## Counting distinct values

After sorting, equal values are next to each other, so you count a new value whenever `a[i] != a[i-1]`. That turns an O(n^2) problem into O(n log n).

## bsearch

The library also has `bsearch` with the same compare function, for searching sorted arrays.

## Keep practicing

Solve small problems daily. Typical next topics: linked lists, stacks and queues, hash tables, recursion, and splitting code into `.h` and `.c` files built with `make` or CMake.

quiz.q: What does binary search require?
quiz.explain: Binary search only works on sorted data.

quiz.q: Two nested loops over n items usually cost:
quiz.explain: n iterations times n iterations.

quiz.q: What should a qsort compare function return when a should come before b?
quiz.explain: Negative means a sorts before b.

exercise.prompt:

Print two lines:
1. the numbers sorted ascending, separated by single spaces
2. `distinct=K` where K is the number of different values

Use `qsort`.
